daily_netflix.caption:
ARCANE officially premiered on Netflix five years ago, on November 6, 2021, introducing one of the greatest animated series ever created and completely changing expectations for video game adaptations.

Based on the world of LEAGUE OF LEGENDS, the series follows sisters Vi and Jinx as their lives are torn apart by the growing conflict between the wealthy city of Piltover and the oppressed underground of Zaun.

Created by Riot Games and animated by Fortiche, ARCANE became an extraordinary success thanks to its breathtaking animation, emotional storytelling, unforgettable characters, and incredible soundtrack. The first season even won four Emmy Awards and nine Annie Awards.

The story concluded with its second season in November 2024, delivering nine more episodes filled with devastating twists, spectacular action, and an emotional conclusion to Vi and Jinx's complicated relationship.

Five years later, ARCANE remains one of Netflix's greatest achievements in animation. With just 18 episodes across two seasons, it managed to tell a story that was visually stunning, emotionally heartbreaking, and genuinely unforgettable. An absolute masterpiece from beginning to end.

Jane Fonda champions Democrats and the "blue tsunami" after huge Election Day wins over the Republican party: 

"I’m just so proud of American people, that they were paying attention and it wasn’t just about affordability. [James] Talarico’s acceptance speech was a masterpiece and in it he said, ‘We voted to love our neighbor’... [Now] we have to be very smart. We can’t return to the old neoliberalism. We have to take off our corporate hat, take off our donor hat, and start doing things that are going to help working people in this country, and we have to rule with love. नेपालमा गैरकानुनी रूपमा बस्ने, काम गर्ने तथा विभिन्न आपराधिक गतिविधिमा संलग्न भएको अभियोगमा बाङ्ग्लादेशी नागरिकको पक्राउ र निष्कासन बढ्दै गएको छ। सरकारी तथ्याङ्कअनुसार चिनियाँ नागरिकपछि नेपालबाट सबैभन्दा धेरै निष्कासन हुने विदेशी नागरिकमा बाङ्ग्लादेशी छन्।

बीबीसी नेपालीका अनुसार पछिल्लो १० महिनामा ८६ जना बाङ्ग्लादेशी नागरिकलाई नेपालबाट निष्कासन गरिएको छ। पछिल्लो साउनदेखि असोजसम्मको चार महिनामा मात्रै ५१ जना निष्कासनमा परेका छन्। हाल अध्यागमन विभागको हिरासतमा १८ जना बाङ्ग्लादेशी नागरिक छन्।

कार्तिक १६ गते काठमाडौंका विभिन्न स्थानबाट चार बाङ्ग्लादेशी र एक भारतीय नागरिक पक्राउ परेका थिए। उनीहरूलाई थप अनुसन्धानका लागि अध्यागमन विभागमा बुझाइएको छ। यसअघि पनि अवैध रूपमा बसोबास गरेको, अनुमतिबिना काम गरेको र शङ्कास्पद गतिविधिमा संलग्न भएको अभियोगमा बाङ्ग्लादेशी नागरिक पक्राउ परेका थिए।

प्रहरीका अनुसार केही नागरिक पर्यटक भिसामा नेपाल आएर काम गर्ने, भिसाको म्याद सकिएपछि पनि बस्ने वा अवैध बाटोबाट प्रवेश गर्ने गरेको पाइएको छ। अनलाइन ठगीलगायत आपराधिक गतिविधिमा संलग्न भएको आशङ्कामा समेत अनुसन्धान भइरहेको अधिकारीहरूले बताएका छन्।

प्रहरीले दिएको तथ्याङ्कअनुसार पछिल्लो एक वर्षमा हवाई मार्गबाट १ लाख १७ हजार ६८२ बाङ्ग्लादेशी नागरिक नेपाल आएका वा फर्किएका छन्। तीमध्ये ५८ हजार ८७९ जना नेपाल भित्रिएका र ५८ हजार ८०३ जना फर्किएका छन्।

अध्यागमन विभागले भिसा उल्लङ्घन गर्नेहरूबाट आवश्यक शुल्क र जरिवाना असुल गरी केही वर्ष नेपाल प्रवेशमा रोक लगाएर निष्कासन गर्ने गरेको जनाएको छ। आपराधिक गतिविधिमा संलग्न भएको पुष्टि भएमा भने सम्बन्धित कानुनअनुसार कारबाही हुने अधिकारीहरूको भनाइ छ।

राष्ट्रिय स्वतन्त्र पार्टी (रास्वपा)का सभापति रवि लामिछानेले पार्टीभित्र बढ्दै गएको अहङ्कार, अवसरवादी चरित्र र आन्तरिक ईर्ष्या त्याग्न नेता तथा कार्यकर्तालाई निर्देशन दिएका छन्।

शुक्रबार चितवनमा आयोजित पार्टीको आन्तरिक प्रशिक्षण कार्यक्रममा बोल्दै लामिछानेले जनताले दिएको मतलाई अहङ्कारमा बदल्न नहुने बताए। पार्टीले सफलता हासिल गरेपछि केही नेता–कार्यकर्तामा घमण्ड बढेको उल्लेख गर्दै उनले जनताको सेवक भएर काम गर्न आग्रह गरे।

उनले वडाध्यक्षको चुनाव लड्न नचाहने तर एकैपटक मेयर र सांसद बन्न खोज्ने प्रवृत्तिप्रति असन्तुष्टि जनाए। शक्तिको आडमा प्रहरी तथा प्रशासनलाई दबाब दिने राजनीति रास्वपाको नभएको पनि उनले स्पष्ट पारे।

आगामी निर्वाचनमा उम्मेदवार छनोट पार्टीको विधि र आन्तरिक निर्वाचन प्रणालीबाटै हुने भन्दै उनले भनसुन वा नेतासँगको निकटताका आधारमा टिकट नपाइने बताए। टिकट नपाएको भन्दै पार्टीलाई धोका दिने वा विपक्षीसँग मिल्ने प्रवृत्ति स्वीकार्य नहुने उनको भनाइ थियो।

लामिछानेले पार्टीको एकता, अनुशासन र पारदर्शितालाई मुख्य शक्ति मान्दै सबै नेता–कार्यकर्तालाई जिम्मेवार भएर अघि बढ्न आग्रह गरेका छन्।

नेपाल इन्फ्रास्ट्रक्चर समिटसम्बन्धी कार्यक्रममा बोल्दै वाग्लेले सरकारले भ्रष्टतन्त्रको सफाइ गर्ने र विगतदेखि कायम राजनीतिक तथा प्रशासनिक अभ्यासमा परिवर्तन ल्याउने दाबी गरे। जुद्धशमशेरपछि कुनै सरकारले पाँच वर्ष पूरा नगरेको उल्लेख गर्दै उनले यसपटक त्यो क्रम तोड्ने बताए।

वाग्लेका अनुसार सरकारले अहिले १६६ वटा ऐनमाथि काम गरिरहेको छ। तीमध्ये ५९ वटा ऐनलाई एउटै प्याकेजमा अघि बढाउने तयारी छ। साथै, आठदेखि १० वटा ठूला पूर्वाधार आयोजना एकैपटक अघि बढाउने सरकारको योजना रहेको उनले जानकारी दिए।

उनले विकासमा निजी क्षेत्रको सहभागिता बढाउने, निजी पुँजी परिचालन गर्ने र वैकल्पिक विकास वित्तसम्बन्धी व्यवस्था कार्यान्वयनमा लैजाने बताए। बाढीपहिरोजस्ता चुनौतीका बाबजुद राजस्व संकलनको गति राम्रो रहेको उल्लेख गर्दै वाग्लेले यसलाई सरकारको सुशासन प्रयासको सकारात्मक परिणामका रूपमा व्याख्या गरे।

Australia Offers Two-Year Training Visa for Foreigners Without Student Visa

Australia's Training Visa (Subclass 407) allows eligible foreign nationals to undertake supervised workplace training and professional development for up to two years without enrolling in a traditional academic programme.

The visa is designed for people seeking to improve their professional skills, gain practical experience or acquire qualifications relevant to their careers. Applicants must have an approved Australian sponsor and meet English-language, health and other immigration requirements.

However, the visa is not a general work permit and is intended specifically for structured occupational training. Applicants must meet all eligibility conditions before applying.

Disturbing Details Emerge in Mamta Kafle Case: Husband Describes Dismembering Her Body

VIRGINIA, USA: In a shocking development in the disappearance and suspected murder case of Nepali nurse Mamta Kafle Bhatt, her husband, Naresh Bhatt, has admitted in court that he dismembered her body after finding her dead inside their bedroom.

During testimony at his murder trial on Thursday, Naresh told the court that he discovered Mamta lying unresponsive on the bedroom floor on the morning of July 30, 2024. He claimed that after finding her, he attempted to check whether she was alive and tried performing life-saving measures, including CPR.

According to his testimony, he noticed vomit around Mamta's mouth and on the bedroom floor. He described the substance as containing blood, food particles, capsules and traces of Celphos, a pesticide.

Naresh further told the court that he subsequently decided to dismember her body. He said he initially attempted to separate the lower part of her body, including her legs, before moving her remains to the bathroom. However, he claimed that he felt physically weak and stopped the process on the first day.

He also described how he used a baby-changing station to block the bedroom doorway before returning to care for their young daughter. He testified that he fed and put the child to sleep but could not sleep himself that night because he was frightened. He also said he avoided going into the prayer room.

Naresh is facing charges including first-degree murder, concealing a body and unlawfully dismembering a human body. Despite his admission about dismembering Mamta's remains, her body has never been recovered.

How the Investigation Began

The investigation started after Mamta, who worked as a nurse at UVA Health Prince William Medical Center in Virginia, failed to show up for work.

Initially, Naresh denied that anything had happened to his wife and reportedly told investigators that he had last seen her on July 29, 2024. However, Mamta's friends and family raised concerns, insisting that she would never voluntarily abandon her young daughter.

Naresh did not report Mamta missing to police until August 5, 2024. During the process, he claimed that she had threatened to leave him and had discussed divorce.

Investigators later discovered blood evidence inside the couple's master bedroom and bathroom. Police also recovered an electric saw with strands of hair caught in it.

Following the discovery of the evidence, Naresh was arrested on August 22, 2024, and has remained in custody since then.

Mamta's Body Has Never Been Found

One of the most disturbing aspects of the case is that investigators have still not recovered Mamta's remains.

Her disappearance shocked Nepal's community in the United States and drew widespread attention from Nepalis at home and abroad. Mamta was a healthcare professional and a mother of a young daughter when she disappeared.

The latest courtroom testimony has brought new details to light about what Naresh claims happened inside their home. However, the circumstances surrounding Mamta's death and the full sequence of events remain central issues in the ongoing murder proceedings.

The case continues to attract attention as the court examines the evidence and Naresh's statements in an effort to establish what happened to Mamta Kafle Bhatt.

Naresh Bhatt, who is facing murder charges in connection with the disappearance of his wife, Nepali nurse Mamta Kafle Bhatt, has denied physically abusing her while testifying in a Virginia court. However, the 39-year-old acknowledged that their marriage had deteriorated and admitted that he had caused her emotional and mental distress. His testimony came on November 4, the 16th day of the trial, after prosecutors completed presenting their evidence.

During questioning, prosecutor Tracy Lennox confronted Bhatt with text messages exchanged between the couple in the months before Mamta disappeared. Bhatt denied threatening her with physical violence but admitted to emotional mistreatment. He said arguments had become frequent from early 2024, with him threatening divorce and Mamta sometimes threatening suicide. He also acknowledged refusing to eat food she prepared and sometimes stopping communication with her. However, earlier testimony from Mamta’s brother and friend described alleged physical abuse, including claims that Mamta had shared photographs of injuries and said she did not feel safe at home.

Bhatt also discussed disputes over money, their relationship problems and Mamta’s temporary stay with her friend Sarita Neupane. Their accounts differed over how long Mamta stayed away from home. Bhatt denied controlling Mamta’s finances, while Sarita testified that she had helped Mamta open separate bank accounts because of concerns about financial control. Bhatt also disputed the prosecution’s interpretation of some Nepali text messages, arguing that translation had affected their meaning.

Mamta disappeared from the couple’s home in Manassas Park, Virginia, in late July 2024, and her body has never been found. Prosecutors allege that Bhatt killed her and disposed of her remains at multiple waste sites in Northern Virginia. They have presented evidence including blood DNA reportedly matching Mamta, a saw containing blood, Google searches, CCTV footage and purchases of cleaning supplies. Bhatt has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder, concealing a body and defiling a body.

Democrats Take Control of Congress, Putting Trump Under Pressure as Iran War, Ukraine Aid and Immigration Policies Face New Challenges

KATHMANDU — Democrats have won control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress, delivering a major political setback to President Donald Trump and creating new challenges for his administration. The Democratic Party's victory in the November 3 midterm elections means Republicans have lost their majority in both the Senate and the House of Representatives. The result will make it harder for Trump to pass new laws and carry out his political agenda during the final two years of his presidency.

The election results reflect growing frustration among American voters over rising living costs, trade policies, immigration restrictions and the war with Iran. Democrats gained several seats in traditionally Republican states and districts, showing that many voters wanted stronger checks on Trump's administration. The victory also gives Democrats greater power to investigate the government, question officials and challenge presidential decisions.

What Does the Democratic Victory Mean for Trump?

The U.S. president has broad powers over foreign policy, national security, trade and immigration. However, Congress plays an important role in checking presidential authority. It approves government spending, passes national laws, investigates government activities and reviews many senior appointments.

With Democrats controlling both chambers, Trump will face stronger opposition when trying to pass new laws or secure funding for his policies. Democratic lawmakers will also lead important congressional committees, giving them greater power to investigate decisions made by the Trump administration.

However, the election result does not mean Trump has lost his presidential powers. He can still issue executive orders and make many decisions on trade, immigration and foreign policy without getting approval from Congress. Democrats can hold hearings, question government officials and challenge his decisions, but they cannot automatically cancel every policy introduced by the president.

The new Congress is expected to begin its work in January 2027. Until then, Republicans will continue to control both chambers, meaning the immediate balance of power in Washington will not change overnight.

Can Democrats Stop Trump's Trade Policies?

Trump's trade policies, especially his decision to impose high tariffs on goods from other countries, have been a major source of disagreement between Republicans and Democrats.

Trump has introduced heavy import taxes on products from both rival nations and long-standing U.S. allies, including Canada. He has argued that tariffs protect American industries and help strengthen the country's economy. However, critics say these policies increase costs for businesses and consumers.

Democrats have repeatedly criticized the tariffs but have struggled to challenge them because Republicans controlled Congress. Their new majority will give them more opportunities to question the administration's trade decisions and examine the economic impact of the tariffs.

However, Trump still has significant authority to impose tariffs through existing trade laws. According to James Smith, a market economist at Dutch bank ING, trade is one area where a president can take action without always needing congressional approval.

Democrats may use public hearings, investigations and other political tools to put pressure on the administration. But ending Trump's existing tariff policies will not be easy.

What Happens to Trump's Immigration Policies?

Immigration is another major issue that could create serious disagreements between Trump and the new Democratic Congress.

Trump has repeatedly defended his strict immigration policies, saying stronger border security is necessary to protect the United States and its citizens. His administration has introduced tougher measures targeting illegal immigration and border crossings.

Democrats have strongly criticized several of these policies, arguing that immigration enforcement should protect human rights and provide fair treatment to migrants.

With control of both chambers, Democrats will have more power to investigate immigration enforcement, question officials and challenge new government proposals. They could also use congressional hearings to examine how immigration laws are being implemented.

However, policies that are already in place will not automatically end because Democrats have won the election. Trump can continue using his executive powers, although new legislation and government funding decisions could become more difficult for his administration.

Can Congress Stop Trump From Going to War?

The war with Iran is expected to become one of the biggest sources of conflict between Trump and the new Democratic Congress.

Democratic lawmakers have repeatedly opposed the administration's military actions against Iran and have questioned whether Trump has sufficient legal authority to continue the conflict without congressional approval.

They have previously introduced three War Powers Resolution measures aimed at limiting Trump's military actions. One proposal passed the House of Representatives with support from some Republicans but failed to gain enough votes in the Senate.

Under the U.S. War Powers Resolution, the president must generally notify Congress within 48 hours of introducing U.S. forces into hostilities. Military action is generally limited to 60 days without congressional authorization, with a possible additional 30-day period for withdrawing forces.

Trump has argued that the military operation against Iran does not amount to a formal war. His administration has used this position to defend its actions without seeking a formal declaration of war from Congress.

Democrats could now increase pressure through investigations, hearings and legislation aimed at limiting military operations. They may also demand greater transparency about the cost, goals and legal basis of the conflict.

However, controlling Congress does not automatically give Democrats the power to stop every military action. The president remains commander in chief, and any major effort to restrict his authority could lead to a serious legal and political battle.

Could U.S. Policy Toward Iran Change?

The election result could also influence Trump's next decisions on Iran.

During the campaign, Trump suggested that the United States could take stronger military action against Iran after the election. However, he has also indicated that negotiations could offer a way to end the conflict.

Democrats have generally opposed expanding the war and have called for greater congressional oversight of military decisions.

Following the election results, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf claimed that American voters had rejected the war against Iran. He said the Iranian government supported the American public's opposition to the conflict and warned that ignoring public opinion could have serious consequences for the United States.

Trump has not announced a major change in his Iran policy following the election. However, the new Democratic majority could make it politically more difficult for his administration to continue military operations without facing strong opposition in Congress.

Will America Resume Military Aid to Ukraine?

U.S. support for Ukraine could also become an important issue under the new congressional majority.

Trump recently halted some American assistance to Ukraine, saying he wants to end the war through negotiations between Russia and Ukraine. His administration has supported efforts to bring the two countries to the negotiating table, including talks expected to take place in Abu Dhabi.

Democrats, however, have generally supported continued military and financial assistance to Ukraine as it defends itself against Russia's invasion.

They have also criticized Trump's approach to negotiations, arguing that Ukraine should not be pressured into accepting an unfair agreement that benefits Russia.

With Democrats controlling both chambers, there could be renewed efforts to approve financial and military assistance for Kyiv. Democratic lawmakers may also use congressional oversight to question the administration's decisions on Ukraine.

The change in Congress could therefore offer Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy greater support in Washington. However, any major change in U.S. policy will depend on negotiations between Congress and the White House, as well as the availability of funding.

Can Democrats Remove Trump From Power?

Although Democrats have won control of Congress, the election does not automatically threaten Trump's position as president.

The president cannot be removed simply because his party loses its majority in the midterm elections. Congress can investigate the administration and begin impeachment proceedings if there are sufficient legal and political grounds. Removing a president through impeachment requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate to convict and remove him from office.

Democrats will not have enough votes to achieve that on their own.

They also cannot easily override a presidential veto. If Trump rejects a bill passed by Congress, lawmakers need a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate to override his decision.

This means Trump will retain important powers even after Democrats take control of Congress. However, his ability to pass new laws and secure support for his policies will face much stronger resistance.

Trump Promises to Work With Democrats

Following the election results, Trump said he was willing to accept the outcome and work with Democrats. He congratulated the opposition party on its victory but rejected the idea that the result was a personal defeat.

Trump also indicated that he could use his presidential veto to block legislation he disagrees with. His comments suggest that cooperation between the White House and Congress may be difficult, especially on major issues such as immigration, trade and foreign policy.

Former President Barack Obama also responded to the election results on social media, saying the outcome could change the country's political direction. He criticized Trump's policies and said American voters wanted political leadership that brought people together rather than divided society.

The Democratic victory marks a major shift in Washington's political balance. Although Trump will remain president and retain significant executive powers, he will now face a Congress controlled by his political opponents. The coming months could bring intense battles over Iran, Ukraine, immigration, trade and government spending as Democrats seek to increase oversight of his administration.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race, making history as the first Muslim elected to the United States Senate. The 42-year-old progressive politician is a former public health official and a strong supporter of universal health care. However, his election victory does not mean he takes office immediately. He will join the Senate when his term officially begins.

Born and raised in southeastern Michigan, El-Sayed is the son of an Egyptian immigrant father. He studied at the University of Michigan, Oxford University, and Columbia University, where he earned degrees in public health and medicine. He previously served as director of the Detroit Health Department and later led the Wayne County Department of Health, Human Services, and Veterans Affairs. His political priorities include affordable health care, reducing living costs, and limiting the influence of wealthy donors in politics.

El-Sayed has clearly supported Ukraine in its war against Russia. Shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, he described the attack as an act of aggression against a democratic country. He praised countries that supported Ukraine by providing weapons and helping refugees. In an August 2026 interview with NBC's Meet the Press, he explained that Ukraine has the right to defend itself against an invasion by another country. He said supporting Ukraine is important for protecting international law and national independence.

His position on Israel is very different. El-Sayed has called for an immediate end to all U.S. military aid to Israel, including both offensive and defensive weapons. He has also supported restoring humanitarian funding for Palestinians, including support for UNRWA, the United Nations agency that helps Palestinian refugees. He has accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza. His position has created strong disagreements among voters, particularly within Michigan's Jewish community.

However, El-Sayed has said that both Palestinians and Israelis have the right to live in peace, dignity, and security. In a November 1, 2026, interview with 60 Minutes, he said Palestine has a right to exist. He also said Israel has a right to exist, while adding that both sides must agree on a fair political arrangement. He supports either a two-state solution or a single shared state if both communities freely choose that arrangement.

El-Sayed has also faced criticism over his comments about Hamas and an attack on a synagogue in Michigan. In October 2025, his campaign sent a fundraising email criticizing Israel's military actions in Gaza without mentioning Hamas's October 7, 2023, attack on Israel. The email drew criticism, although his campaign said it had been sent by mistake. A separate statement released by El-Sayed on the same day condemned Hamas's attack, the killings, and the taking of hostages.

In March 2026, after an attack on Temple Israel synagogue in West Bloomfield, Michigan, El-Sayed condemned the violence and expressed support for the Jewish community. However, his later comments connecting the attack to the wider Middle East conflict angered some members of the community. In August, he apologized for those remarks, saying his initial condemnation should have been enough. He also stated that antisemitism must be opposed in all its forms.

El-Sayed's election has brought renewed attention to his foreign policy views, especially his different positions on Ukraine and Israel. He argues that supporting Ukraine is necessary because Russia invaded a sovereign country, while he opposes U.S. military support for Israel because of its actions in Gaza. However, his campaign statements do not guarantee how he will vote on every foreign aid proposal. His actual decisions on military assistance, funding, and foreign policy will become clearer after he officially takes his seat in the U.S. Senate.

नेपाली कांग्रेसले पार्टी र नेतृत्वविरुद्ध भइरहेको भनिएको षड्यन्त्र, दुष्प्रचार तथा राज्य संयन्त्रको दुरुपयोगविरुद्ध राजनीतिक र कानुनी रूपमा प्रतिवाद गर्ने जनाएको छ। महामन्त्री प्रदीप पौडेलले मंगलबार सार्वजनिक गरेको ६ बुँदे धारणामार्फत पार्टीको वैधानिकतामाथि उठाइएका प्रश्न र विभिन्न प्रचार निराधार तथा नियोजित भएको दाबी गरेका छन्।

कांग्रेसले २०८२ पुसमा सम्पन्न विशेष महाधिवेशन निर्वाचन आयोगबाट अद्यावधिक भइसकेको र सर्वोच्च अदालतबाट समेत वैधानिक ठहर भएको उल्लेख गरेको छ। साथै, २०८३ असोज १६ देखि २३ गतेसम्म १५औँ महाधिवेशन सम्पन्न भइसकेकाले पार्टीको वैधानिकतामाथि प्रश्न उठाउने प्रयास स्वीकार्य नहुने जनाएको छ।

वरिष्ठ उपसभापति विश्वप्रकाश शर्माले बुधबार पत्रकार सम्मेलन गर्दै पार्टी र नेतृत्वविरुद्ध उठेका प्रश्न तथा छानबिनको सामना गर्न तयार रहेको बताए। उनले इनम सापकोटा प्रकरणमा प्रधानमन्त्री कार्यालयसँग सम्बन्धित व्यक्तिहरूको संलग्नतामा अनुसन्धानमा रहेका व्यक्ति र प्रमाणमाथि अनधिकृत नियन्त्रण तथा छेडछाड भएको भनिएका विषयको निष्पक्ष अनुसन्धान हुनुपर्ने माग गरे।

कांग्रेसले प्रहरी महानिरीक्षक हटाउने घटनालाई पनि यही घटनाक्रमसँग जोड्दै राज्य संयन्त्रको दुरुपयोग भएको आरोप लगाएको छ। पत्रकारमाथिको धरपकड, प्रेस नियन्त्रण र संवैधानिक निकायमाथिको हस्तक्षेपप्रति आपत्ति जनाउँदै पार्टीले कानुनी परामर्श र संसदीय पहल अघि बढाउने जनाएको छ।

कांग्रेसले सरकारलाई प्रतिपक्षलाई कमजोर बनाउने गतिविधि बन्द गरी विपद् प्रभावितको राहत, अर्थतन्त्रको पुनरुत्थान र जनसरोकारका विषयमा ध्यान दिन आग्रह गरेको छ।

प्रहरी महानिरीक्षक (आईजीपी) डा. मनोज केसीले दर्ज्यानी चिह्न लगाएका छन्। बुधबार गृह मन्त्रालयमा गृहमन्त्री सुधन गुरुङले उनलाई दर्ज्यानी चिह्न लगाइदिएका हुन्।

केसी बुधबार नै नेपाल प्रहरीको ३४औँ महानिरीक्षकमा नियुक्त भएका थिए। यसअघि आईजीपीलाई गृहसचिवले दर्ज्यानी चिह्न लगाइदिने परम्परा रहे पनि यसपटक गृहमन्त्री आफैँले चिह्न प्रदान गरेका छन्।

The Nepal Tourism Board has announced its first-ever Kukur Tihar Reel Competition 2026, offering a cash prize of Rs. 1 lakh to the winning creator. The competition aims to promote Nepal’s unique Kukur Tihar festival internationally through creative short videos highlighting the cultural significance of the festival and the special bond between humans and dogs.

To participate, creators must publish an original reel publicly on Instagram or Facebook using the hashtags #NepalFestival and #KukurTihar, while tagging the Nepal Tourism Board on the respective platform. The video must be in English or include English subtitles or an English voice-over.

A Saudi-based company has agreed to pay 181,000 Saudi riyals to the family of Bharat Mahato, a 45-year-old Nepali worker from Mahottari who was killed in a drone attack in Saudi Arabia. The amount includes 31,000 riyals in end-of-service benefits and 150,000 riyals in compensation.

The agreement was reached following an initiative by the Nepali Embassy in Riyadh. According to Nepali Labour Counsellor Kabiraj Upreti, the money will be sent to Bharat’s family after the necessary administrative procedures are completed. The company agreed to provide the compensation on humanitarian grounds after learning that Bharat’s labour permit had expired, potentially making his family ineligible for financial assistance from Nepal’s Foreign Employment Board and insurance.

Bharat had worked for the company for 14 years and was employed at an oil project operated by Saudi Aramco. He was killed on Kartik 4 in a drone attack targeting the Shaybah oil field in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province. The attack, attributed to Yemen’s Houthi rebels, also killed a Filipino worker.

Bharat was the main financial support for his family and had been building a house near his hometown. His wife is now facing the responsibility of raising their four children while dealing with an outstanding bank loan. Although the Nepali Embassy has completed the necessary procedures to bring his body home, flight disruptions have delayed its return, and the arrival date remains uncertain.

#BharatMahato #NepaliWorkers #SaudiArabia #DroneAttack #NepalNews #HouthiAttack

बुधबार बसेको मन्त्रिपरिषद् बैठकपछि सञ्चारकर्मीसँग कुरा गर्दै मन्त्री पोखरेलले बदलिँदो परिस्थितिका कारण पार्टीबाट सरकारलाई संवेदनशील विषयमा आवश्यक कदम चाल्न निर्देशन आएको बताएका हुन्।

‘धेरै ठाउँबाट अहिले बदलिँदो परिस्थिति छ । पार्टीबाट पनि संवेदनशील विषयमा सरकारले केही गर्नुपर्‍यो भनेर निर्देशन आएको थियो,’ मन्त्री पोखरेलले भने, ‘त्यसपछि जिम्मेवारी हेरफेर गरिएको हो।’

उनले प्रधानमन्त्रीलाई शान्ति सुरक्षासम्बन्धी सल्लाह दिने जिम्मेवारी पनि निकै संवेदनशील हुने उल्लेख गरे। यस्तो जिम्मेवारीको महत्वलाई ध्यानमा राखेर निर्णय गरिएको उनको भनाइ थियो।

सरकारको यो अभिव्यक्तिले नेपाल प्रहरीको नेतृत्व परिवर्तनमा पार्टीको निर्देशनले भूमिका खेलेको विषयलाई थप चर्चामा ल्याएको छ।

A 16-year study has revealed that West Coast Bigg’s killer whales are divided into two distinct communities: inner coast and outer coast.

Researchers from the University of British Columbia analyzed more than 2,200 encounters and discovered that these groups rarely meet, despite overlapping in their geographic range.

Inner coast orcas generally stay closer to shore, hunting animals such as harbour seals and harbour porpoises. Outer coast orcas spend more time in deeper waters near the continental shelf, targeting larger marine mammals.

The two communities meet in less than one percent of recorded sightings. Researchers believe their different habitats, prey preferences, and possibly human activities may help explain this separation.

The discovery highlights why conservation strategies must consider the different needs of each orca community.

Source: Discover Wildlife, November 10, 2025; University of British Columbia study published in PLOS ONE.

#Wildlife #AnimalLovers #Nature

The real story: On October 16, 2026, crews with Vancouver Island Whale Watch in Nanaimo, British Columbia, watched a Bigg's killer whale known as T037B1, "Lance," moonwalk, surfacing backward, in the Strait of Georgia, after what looked like a successful hunt. The behavior is attributed to Bigg's orcas and is thought to be linked to dividing up prey. Source: Vancouver Island Whale Watch, October 16, 2026.

It looks like a dance move, and it isn't. On October 16, 2026, whale watchers in the Strait of Georgia off Nanaimo, British Columbia, watched a Bigg's killer whale known as Lance, catalogued T037B1, flick his tail up out of the water and move backward across the surface. The crew called it a moonwalk.

Moonwalking is a behavior attributed to Bigg's orcas, the mammal-eating kind found along British Columbia's coast. Marine zoologist Anna Hall told CBC it is "a little bit gruesome": the whale may be tearing the prey into pieces to share with family members. The crew on Oct. 16 missed the hunt itself, but the whales were making longer dives and slapping their tails, clues that they had recently caught a meal. Bigg's orcas are cooperative hunters, and a successful hunt can feed several members of a family, with prey sharing an important part of their social life.

One whale in particular is known for the move. T65A, called Artemis, born in 1986, has been seen moonwalking after killing harbour porpoises. Experts say it isn't clear whether the technique is used for any one type of prey. What's clear is that when you see an orca moving backward at the surface, you are probably watching a family dinner.

Follow Blue Depths for more real ocean moments, captured as they happen.

#BlueDepth #Orca #BiggsOrca #Moonwalking #BritishColumbia #AnimalBehavior

Along the Atlantic coasts of Spain and Portugal, orcas continue to interact with small sailboats and yachts, sometimes striking or damaging their rudders.

Researchers believe these encounters may be linked to social play or learned behavior rather than deliberate aggression toward humans. However, the exact reasons behind the interactions remain uncertain.

Although the encounters can leave boats damaged and crews frightened, scientists continue studying this unusual behavior to better understand why some orcas approach vessels.

#Wildlife #AnimalLovers #Nature

President Donald Trump has confirmed that the United States military carried out a targeted precision airstrike inside Iranian territory, moving quickly to downplay concerns that the operation signaled a broader military conflict.

Speaking to reporters, Trump characterized the operation as a localized tactical response rather than a major escalation, stating directly that the mission was just a small strike and not a war. According to defense officials and regional reports, the precision strike targeted an Iranian surface-to-air missile radar installation on Qeshm Island along the strategic Strait of Hormuz. The targeted facility, which had been under construction for roughly two months, was struck after intelligence indicated it was being positioned to track and target American and allied aerial assets operating across international airspace.

While regional tensions remain exceptionally high following months of heightened confrontation in the Persian Gulf, the White House emphasized that the action was narrowly calibrated to eliminate an immediate defensive hazard without triggering a wider regional exchange. Iranian authorities have acknowledged damage to radar infrastructure while continuing to protest foreign military activity in the Gulf waterways.

As international markets and defense analysts closely monitor the Persian Gulf for potential retaliatory moves, Washington has signaled that deterrence remains active while leaving open diplomatic avenues for de-escalation.

In an extraordinary disclosure highlighting the cutthroat geopolitical race for artificial intelligence dominance, United States intelligence agencies have concluded that China’s premier civilian spy agency targeted Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang through an orchestrated human espionage operation.

According to classified intelligence briefings and internal memos circulated among senior national security policymakers, Beijing’s Ministry of State Security recruited a Chinese businesswoman who had established a close personal and romantic relationship with Huang. Operating under commercial cover linked to international data center ventures, the operative was tasked by Chinese intelligence handlers with gathering sensitive technical insights into Nvidia’s cutting-edge graphics processing architectures and attempting to influence corporate channels regarding strict U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.

As the primary architect behind the hardware powering global artificial intelligence models, Nvidia occupies the epicenter of American technological sovereignty and military capability. While company spokespersons emphasized that cloud partners never receive classified information and do not shape federal policy stances, the revelations have triggered immediate alarm on Capitol Hill. House Republican leaders have officially summoned Huang for closed-door congressional intelligence briefings to assess potential security vulnerabilities and evaluate foreign influence operations targeting America’s most critical semiconductor leadership.

#Nvidia #TechEspionage #NationalSecurity

The battle of Midway was won before a single B*mb fell — in a basement in Hawaii, by Joseph Rochefort and his codebreakers. His team at Station HYPO cracked enough of the Japanese fleet code to prove Midway was the target, letting Nimitz set the perfect ambush.

Rochefort never got the credit in his lifetime. Office politics pushed him aside, and his work stayed classified for decades. The Navy finally awarded him the Distinguished Service Medal in 1986 — ten years after his death. The codebreaker who saved the Pacific got his salute at last.

#JosephRochefort #Codebreaker #Midway #StationHYPO #WWIIHistory

Be honest  should every data center in America be legally required to publicly disclose exactly how much water and electricity it consumes each year?

Across the country, the rapid explosion of artificial intelligence and hyperscale cloud infrastructure is driving an unprecedented surge in resource consumption. From Virginia and Texas to Arizona and Georgia, massive server campuses operate around the clock, drawing millions of gallons of water daily for evaporative cooling towers while placing immense strain on regional electrical grids.

Yet despite their massive footprint, many tech conglomerates keep their facility-level utility data tightly guarded under non-disclosure agreements with municipal utility providers. Local residents, agricultural communities, and small business owners frequently face higher utility rates or water conservation warnings while remaining entirely in the dark about how much local capacity is diverted to power AI clusters.

Advocates argue that transparency is a matter of basic public accountability. When public aquifers, regional watersheds, and taxpayer-backed power grids are at stake, citizens deserve to know the real cost of keeping the digital economy running.

Conversely, tech developers contend that detailed consumption figures constitute proprietary operational data that could expose server capacity and competitive trade secrets to rival firms.

Don’t Americans deserve to know the true footprint of the data centers operating in their backyards?

What do you think?

#DataCenters #TechNews #Energy

A 26-year-old Venezuelan national who entered the United States illegally is in federal custody after being apprehended by the U.S. Secret Service near the White House with a cache of weapons, telling investigators that voices in his head instructed him to travel to Washington to kill President Donald Trump.

According to federal affidavits and statements released by the Department of Homeland Security, officers approached Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chirinos around 11:42 p.m. Thursday as he was asleep inside a parked Ford F-150 on Constitution Avenue. The vehicle had previously been reported stolen. What began as a routine welfare check rapidly escalated when Guanipa Chirinos used Google Translate on his mobile phone to inform officers that he had firearms in the truck that he wanted to turn over to authorities.

Upon searching the vehicle, Secret Service personnel recovered a disassembled AR-15 style rifle, a MAC-10 handgun, a Glock 43X pistol, extended magazines, and dozens of rounds of loose and boxed ammunition. During subsequent questioning, the suspect stated that he had been living in the stolen truck, purchased the weapons roughly a month prior, and drove to the nation’s capital following internal auditory hallucinations commanding him to assassinate the president.

Records confirm Guanipa Chirinos crossed the southern border unlawfully near Eagle Pass, Texas, in March 2024, where he was processed by Border Patrol and released into the interior. Following his arrest, Immigration and Customs Enforcement lodged an immigration detainer with the U.S. Marshals Service, where he remains held on multiple federal weapons charges.

#BreakingNews #WhiteHouse #SecretService

"Bull" Halsey was the fighting face of the Pacific war — aggressive, profane, beloved by his sailors. His motto said it all: "Hit hard, hit fast, hit often." When he took the Third Fleet into the Battle of Leyte Gulf in 1944, it became the largest naval battle in history.

He made mistakes, and he knew it. But no one ever doubted his heart. When Japan surrendered, Halsey was there on the Missouri's deck, watching the war he had sworn to win come to its end.

#BullHalsey #LeyteGulf #USNavy #PacificWar #WWIIHistory

He was the Navy's quiet genius — a cruiser sailor with no aviation background who ended up commanding the carriers at the most important naval battle of the war. At Midway, Raymond Spruance made the cold, perfect calls: launch everything, keep the carriers moving, don't get drawn in. Four Japanese carriers went to the bottom.

Two years later he did it again at the Philippine Sea, destroying Japan's carrier air power for good. He never sought glory, never wrote memoirs, never bragged. His fellow admirals just called him the finest naval commander of the war.

#RaymondSpruance #Midway #USNavy #PacificWar #WWIIHistory

Afghanistan Combat Veteran Urges Women To Protect American Freedom

Serving as a military police team leader across 40 months of deployment in Afghanistan, the veteran recalls being the sole female service member in her convoys, tasked with conducting security searches of local Afghan women and witnessing firsthand the complete absence of legal autonomy and basic human rights under strict Sharia governance

In Her Own Words

“I was usually the ONLY WOMAN in my convoy in Afghanistan. Not only was I a military police team leader, I was the one who searched the Afghan women. Those women told me things their husbands never would. They also told me things they wouldn't tell their husbands. They let me hold their babies and talk to their kids. These women had NO voice in that country. No rights. They were men's property. 40 months in a Muslim country taught me this: Sharia doesn't 'coexist.' It TAKES. And here in the USA, it will take from women FIRST. Ladies, it starts with your voice. DO NOT hand it over. It wasn't very long ago at all that we fought for and WON our freedom here in America. We owe it to our daughters not to go backwards.”

The Lakewood Police Department has officially identified the officer killed in the line of duty during Thursday night’s shooting as Agent Nic Graham.

Agent Graham, badge number 2150, joined the department in 2019 after graduating from the academy. Over five years of dedicated service to the city of Lakewood, he earned widespread respect among his peers, including being honored with the department’s Special Investigations Unit Wingman Award in 2023 for exemplary teamwork and tactical support.

The tragic confrontation unfolded around 6:30 PM on Thursday, November 5, when Lakewood agents tracked an armed suspect boarding an RTD transit bus near Colfax Avenue and Wadsworth Boulevard. As officers moved in to make contact, the suspect immediately opened fire.

Agents returned fire and neutralized the gunman on scene. During the intense close-quarters shootout, four Lakewood police agents and one civilian bystander were struck by gunfire. Agent Graham was rushed to the hospital with catastrophic injuries where he tragically succumbed to his wounds.

Law enforcement agencies, first responders, and community members across Colorado have joined in mourning the loss of a courageous public servant who made the ultimate sacrifice while running toward danger to protect innocent transit riders.

How can communities best honor the families and fellow officers of those who make the ultimate sacrifice in the line of duty?

#NicGraham #LakewoodPolice #LineOfDuty

Newly released security footage has revealed the terrifying split-second gunfight where an armed U.S. Marine Corps veteran confronted and neutralized an active shooter inside a massive corporate office campus in Tampa, Florida.

The suspect, identified by law enforcement as 35-year-old Jacob Pearson of Orlando, drove onto the Citibank Center campus armed with a rifle, a handgun, and roughly 90 rounds of ammunition. Investigators revealed Pearson was enraged over an impending court summons regarding an unpaid 2,500 dollar credit card debt.

After ramming his vehicle through a security fence into a courtyard where employees were eating lunch, Pearson shot and killed beloved nine-year Citibank human resources specialist LeAnne Selman.

With his rifle raised and additional ammunition ready, Pearson then advanced directly toward the cafeteria building, sending thousands of terrified employees running for exits or barricading inside offices, breakrooms, and supply closets across the campus.

Stationed inside the facility was John Fraley, a Citibank security officer, vice president of operations, and combat-trained Marine Corps veteran. Rather than retreating, Fraley immediately moved toward the gunfire.

Taking up a tactical position around a hallway corner near the cafeteria entrance, Fraley drew his service handgun and waited for the intruder to breach the doorway. The harrowing surveillance video captured the exact moment Pearson stepped into the hallway with his rifle in hand. In a fraction of a second, Fraley leaned around the wall, engaged the suspect through heavy muzzle flash, and struck Pearson five times during a rapid exchange of gunfire.

Pearson collapsed and was later pronounced dead after being transported to Tampa General Hospital.

Hillsborough County Sheriff Chad Chronister praised Fraley as an absolute hero who ran directly toward lethal danger and relied on years of military conditioning to save the lives of over 3,200 employees on site.

When faced with an armed active shooter, how critical is prior military training in overriding fear to make split-second life-or-death decisions?

#MarineVeteran #Hero #Tampa

On December 31, 1941, with Pearl Harbor still smoking, Chester Nimitz took command of a broken Pacific Fleet — most of its battleships on the harbor floor. The quiet Texan didn't panic. He listened to his codebreakers, trusted his carrier admirals, and gambled everything on one battle: Midway.

He won. From that June morning in 1942, the tide never turned back. Nimitz ran the largest ocean war in history from a headquarters in Hawaii, island-hopping across the Pacific for three more years until he stood on the deck of the USS Missouri and signed the surrender that ended it.

Medal of Honor recipient Sgt. Maj. Thomas Payne, an operator with the Army's SMU, poses with agents from the Diplomatic Security Service. DSS is the security and law enforcement arm of the U.S. Department of State, responsible for protecting American diplomats, embassies, and personnel in some of the most dangerous places in the world.

Payne received the Medal of Honor for his actions on October 22, 2015, when he helped rescue about 70 hostages facing execution at an ISIS prison near Hawija, Iraq, going back into a burning building under fire to free them.

The special operations and diplomatic security communities may wear different badges, but their missions often overlap. Both operate in high-risk environments, and both are built on the same principle: protecting others, no matter the danger.

The US Army is testing a clever new way to get more out of a cheap drone, and the real innovation is a device about the size of your hand.

It's called MALET, and it's basically a clip-on adapter for standard mortar rounds, the kind soldiers already carry. Snap it onto a 60mm or 81mm round and a drone can carry it aloft and drop it accurately on a target. The genius part: it pops right back off, so the same round can later be used in a regular mortar as if nothing happened.

That solves a real problem. Rigging explosive rounds to drones in the field is dangerous, because it means messing with the safety mechanisms built into them. MALET avoids all of that.

In recent tests, drones dropped 60mm rounds on target at Fort Hood and Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst. 

The drone gets the attention, but the breakthrough is the little clip that makes it work.

General Lemuel Shepherd was the 20th Commandant of the Marine Corps — and the man who led the Corps through the entire Korean War. It was Shepherd who fought to keep Marine aviation under Marine control, who built the Corps back up for Korea, and who watched his Marines hold at Pusan, land at Inchon, and break out of Chosin.

A Marine since 1917, Shepherd had seen the Corps grow from a few thousand men into a force that could turn a war. Korea was his final test, and the Corps passed it.

Twentieth Commandant. First in the hearts of the Marines he led.

The White House has officially declared that it is the formal policy of the United States government to recognize only two genders, male and female.

In a public announcement shared across official administration channels, leadership reaffirmed the strict biological standard across all executive branch operations. The directive reinforces sweeping federal guidelines that govern how government agencies handle official identity records, civil rights enforcement, and federally funded programs nationwide.

Under this policy framework, all federal departments are required to define biological sex rather than gender identity on official documents, passports, and employee records. The administration also mandates strict sex-based distinctions in federal prisons, domestic violence shelters, and intimate government spaces, explicitly reversing prior federal policies.

The move has ignited fierce national debate. Supporters praise the announcement as a common-sense return to biological truth that protects women's spaces and sports, while civil rights organizations and LGBTQ+ advocacy groups argue the policy severely rolls back legal protections for transgender and non-binary Americans.

Before Apollo 11, Buzz Aldrin was a fighter pilot over Korea. Flying F-86 Sabres in 1952, he completed sixty-six combat missions and shot down two MiG-15s over MiG Alley — earning a reputation as a precise, aggressive pilot in the war's toughest air arena.

Aldrin brought an engineer's mind to dogfighting, studying gun-camera film the way he'd later study orbital mechanics. The discipline was the same. Only the altitude changed.

Sixty-six missions over Korea. Then one small step. The fighter pilot came first.

#BuzzAldrin #KoreanWar #USAF #MiGAlley #NeverForget

Kirk Spradley built a career that took him from the Marine Corps to some of the most dangerous contracting work of the Iraq War. A former Force Reconnaissance Marine who also served in the National Guard, he went on to work as a Blackwater contractor and later as a paramilitary officer.

In 2005, he was in Ramadi during some of the heaviest fighting of the war. At the time, the city was one of the most violent places in Iraq, and contractors there worked in the same streets, under the same threats, as the troops around them.

He later wrote about his experiences in his book, "War Junkie: A Cautionary Tale." As the title suggests, it's not a story that glorifies combat. It's a look at what that life gives a man, what it takes from him, and how hard it can be to walk away.

Before he walked on the moon, Neil Armstrong flew combat over Korea. As a Navy ensign flying F9F Panthers off the USS Essex in 1951, he flew seventy-eight combat missions — and once brought his jet home with half a wing torn off after clipping a cable, ejecting over friendly territory.

The calm that steadied a moon landing was forged over Korea. Armstrong rarely talked about the war. He didn't have to. The men who flew with him remembered a pilot who never panicked, not once.

The moon gets the glory. Korea got the making of the man.

#NeilArmstrong #KoreanWar #USNavy #NeverForget #Hero

Two women have advanced further through Navy SEAL training than any women before them. An enlisted sailor and a naval officer entered Basic Underwater Demolition/SEAL training at Coronado several weeks ago, and both made it to the third week, with Hell Week beginning in the fourth.

Neither completed the course. The officer was rolled back to the next class and later asked to be dropped before Hell Week began, while the enlisted sailor was medically pulled during Hell Week itself. Even so, no woman had reached that point since special operations training opened to women in 2016. Their names are being withheld for security and privacy reasons.

The numbers show why every week counts. Navy data from 1998 to 2023 shows that about 68% of all candidates wash out at some stage of the pipeline, and roughly half of all candidates drop before Hell Week even begins. The standard is the same for everyone who shows up, and BUD/S has been breaking candidates of every background for decades.

SHOULD FIREARM SAFETY BE TAUGHT IN EVERY PUBLIC CLASSROOM? Tennessee has become the first state in the nation to mandate annual firearm safety classes for all public and charter school students from kindergarten through 12th grade. The landmark law aims to eliminate accidental childhood shootings by removing the dangerous curiosity around guns and teaching kids exactly what to do if they find an unsecured weapon.

“It will save kids, to be honest with you. It avoids some really bad situations. If we teach children from an early age never to touch a firearm and immediately alert an adult, we take away the curiosity that leads to tragedy.”

 Officer Chad Gann, Wildlife Officer & Firearm Instructor, Tennessee Department of Safety & Homeland Security

How the New Law Works
Statewide Annual Mandate: Under Tennessee Code Ann. § 49-6-1016, all public school districts and charter academies across Tennessee must deliver yearly age-appropriate firearm safety lessons developed in partnership with the Department of Education and the Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency (TWRA).

Elementary Curriculum (Grades K–5): Younger children focus strictly on accident avoidance and identifying real firearms versus toys. Lessons reinforce the foundational four-step rule: Stop, don't touch, leave the area, and immediately tell a trusted adult.

Middle & High School Curriculum (Grades 6–12): Older students study safe storage practices, the mechanical risks of handling firearms, hunter safety fundamentals, suicide prevention awareness, and the legal consequences of unlawful possession.

The state statute strictly prohibits live ammunition or working firearms during instruction. Certified School Resource Officers (SROs) and instructors use inert plastic training props, multimedia presentations, and classroom demonstrations.

Supporters emphasize that with over 400 million firearms in circulation across the United States, basic firearm safety is a vital life skill comparable to teaching kids how to swim, look both ways before crossing the street, or practice fire drills. Demystifying guns reduces accidental discharges caused by childish curiosity.

Critics and gun reform advocates contend that the burden of gun safety belongs exclusively on adult gun owners through strict safe-storage laws, arguing that mandatory school instruction risks normalizing weapons in learning environments.

Francis "Gabby" Gabreski was already a legend before Korea — America's top ace in Europe in World War II with twenty-eight victories. Then he went to Korea and did it again, scoring six and a half more in an F-86 Sabre to become one of only seven Americans to make ace in two wars.

Gabreski flew like he had nothing to prove and everything to give. His total of thirty-four and a half victories stood as the American record for years.

Two wars. Thirty-four and a half. Gabby didn't need a second act — he just kept flying the first one.

#FrancisGabreski #KoreanWar #FlyingAce #USAF #NeverForget

When active gunfire erupted outside his apartment complex near Fort Liberty, Sergeant Brian Lieberman did not barricade his door or wait for backup. An 82nd Airborne Division combat medic, Lieberman sprinted unarmed straight into the courtyard, located a woman suffering from a sucking chest wound, and immediately constructed an airtight seal out of everyday plastic wrap and tape to prevent her lung from collapsing while keeping her stable until civilian paramedics arrived.

According to the official cohort announcement from the Air Force Medical Service, Lieberman was named a 2026 Angel of the Battlefield for his lifesaving actions.

The combat lifesaver instinct never turns off in civilian life. What is your reaction to this paratrooper's composure under fire?

November is National Veterans and Military Family Appreciation month. 

We want to thank our military families for the tremendous contribution they make in supporting of our Soldiers, the mission and the nation.

Senior Chief Special Warfare Operator Andrew Craig Honeyman enlisted at just 17 years old, earned his coveted Navy SEAL Trident at 20, and dedicated over two decades of his life to elite Naval Special Warfare before passing away on April 12, 2026, at age 39.

 Born and raised in Portland, Oregon, Honeyman earned his Trident in June 2007, serving with SEAL Team 5 across Iraq, Afghanistan, Yemen, and Africa before becoming a BUD/S instructor. He later conquered the military’s most demanding selection pipeline to join the Naval Special Warfare Development Group (DEVGRU)—rising to Senior Chief and team leader while executing high-stakes, direct-action missions.

A decorated sniper and parachute tandem master, Honeyman earned three Bronze Star Medals with Combat "V" for Valor alongside numerous commendations. True to the ethos of the quiet professional, he never spoke of his combat accolades, quietly completing his undergraduate degree summa cum laude on active duty and pursuing graduate studies at Georgetown University following his retirement in August 2025.

Behind a stellar career lay the heavy toll of prolonged combat deployments. As his family noted, Andrew fought his internal battles silently and stoically until post-military trauma tragically claimed his life. “SHOT IN THE HELMET AND ARM, HE RIGGED WEBBING TO LOWER FOUR PARALYZED TEAMMATES DOWN A 60-FOOT CLIFF.”

On April 6, 2008, during the Battle of Shok Valley in the rugged Nuristan Province of Afghanistan, Special Forces Operational Detachment Alpha 3336 (ODA 3336, 3rd Special Forces Group) walked into an ambush of catastrophic proportions.

Over 200 entrenched enemy fighters held the high ground on terraced cliffs, raining down relentless machine-gun, sniper, and RPG fire. The assault element was trapped on a narrow, 100-foot ridge, taking catastrophic casualties.

Down at the base of the mountain, Special Forces Medical Sergeant Ronald J. Shurer II didn’t hesitate. Under heavy fire, he charged up the steep, snow-covered rocky incline to reach his pinned-down teammates.

What followed across the next six hours stands as one of the greatest feats of combat medicine in American military history:

 While treating a critically wounded commando, an enemy sniper round struck the back of Shurer’s helmet with concussive force. He shook off the impact and continued treating casualties until another bullet struck his arm. Ignoring his own wounds, he refused to stop.

Shurer stabilized multiple Green Berets and Afghan Commandos who had suffered catastrophic trauma, including severed limbs, traumatic brain injuries, and paralysis, all while exposed on the sheer face of the mountain.

Facing imminent encirclement, Shurer rigged nylon tubular webbing around rocks and trees. Under direct enemy fire, he manually lowered four paralyzed and critically injured teammates down a 60-foot near-vertical cliff, using his own body as a physical shield to deflect incoming rounds and falling rock debris.

Shurer then helped carry the wounded across a freezing, raging river to the medevac landing zone, continuing to treat patients until every man was evacuated. Because of his actions, not a single American died on that mountain.

President Donald J. Trump presented Ronald J. Shurer II with the Medal of Honor on October 1, 2018.

After leaving the Army, Shurer continued his service to the nation as a Special Agent on the U.S. Secret Service Counter Assault Team (CAT). In May 2020, he tragically passed away from stage 4 lung cancer at the age of 41, leaving behind his wife Miranda and two young sons.

A true Green Beret. A warrior medic. An American hero.

After nearly 60 years, the Vietnam-era Hueys that have served the Washington, D.C., area are starting to retire, and their replacement has just arrived.

In an early-November ceremony at Joint Base Andrews, the first of 26 HH-60W Jolly Green II helicopters touched down, flown straight from Sikorsky's plant in Connecticut. It is the first new rotary-wing aircraft to call the D.C. area home in almost six decades.

The upgrade is significant. Compared with the aging UH-1N Huey, the Jolly Green II has a larger airframe, carries far more fuel, flies faster and farther, and offers about three times the airlift capability. And unlike the Hueys' blue, white, and gold paint, the new aircraft will stay gray.

"This mission deserves the modern capability and safety upgrades that are available today," said Col. Karl W. Seekamp, who called the transition a "monumental milestone."

The handover will take years, with full operational capability expected by 2030. But after 60 years, a new chapter has begun.

SHOULD FIREARM SAFETY BE TAUGHT IN EVERY PUBLIC CLASSROOM? Tennessee has become the first state in the nation to mandate annual firearm safety classes for all public and charter school students from kindergarten through 12th grade. The landmark law aims to eliminate accidental childhood shootings by removing the dangerous curiosity around guns and teaching kids exactly what to do if they find an unsecured weapon.

“It will save kids, to be honest with you. It avoids some really bad situations. If we teach children from an early age never to touch a firearm and immediately alert an adult, we take away the curiosity that leads to tragedy.”

 Officer Chad Gann, Wildlife Officer & Firearm Instructor, Tennessee Department of Safety & Homeland Security

How the New Law Works
Statewide Annual Mandate: Under Tennessee Code Ann. § 49-6-1016, all public school districts and charter academies across Tennessee must deliver yearly age-appropriate firearm safety lessons developed in partnership with the Department of Education and the Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency (TWRA).

Elementary Curriculum (Grades K–5): Younger children focus strictly on accident avoidance and identifying real firearms versus toys. Lessons reinforce the foundational four-step rule: Stop, don't touch, leave the area, and immediately tell a trusted adult.

Middle & High School Curriculum (Grades 6–12): Older students study safe storage practices, the mechanical risks of handling firearms, hunter safety fundamentals, suicide prevention awareness, and the legal consequences of unlawful possession.

The state statute strictly prohibits live ammunition or working firearms during instruction. Certified School Resource Officers (SROs) and instructors use inert plastic training props, multimedia presentations, and classroom demonstrations.

Supporters emphasize that with over 400 million firearms in circulation across the United States, basic firearm safety is a vital life skill comparable to teaching kids how to swim, look both ways before crossing the street, or practice fire drills. Demystifying guns reduces accidental discharges caused by childish curiosity.

Critics and gun reform advocates contend that the burden of gun safety belongs exclusively on adult gun owners through strict safe-storage laws, arguing that mandatory school instruction risks normalizing weapons in learning environments.

On April 6, 2008, during the Battle of Shok Valley in the rugged Nuristan Province of Afghanistan, Special Forces Operational Detachment Alpha 3336 (ODA 3336, 3rd Special Forces Group) walked into an ambush of catastrophic proportions.

Over 200 entrenched enemy fighters held the high ground on terraced cliffs, raining down relentless machine-gun, sniper, and RPG fire. The assault element was trapped on a narrow, 100-foot ridge, taking catastrophic casualties.

Down at the base of the mountain, Special Forces Medical Sergeant Ronald J. Shurer II didn’t hesitate. Under heavy fire, he charged up the steep, snow-covered rocky incline to reach his pinned-down teammates.

What followed across the next six hours stands as one of the greatest feats of combat medicine in American military history:

 While treating a critically wounded commando, an enemy sniper round struck the back of Shurer’s helmet with concussive force. He shook off the impact and continued treating casualties until another bullet struck his arm. Ignoring his own wounds, he refused to stop.

Shurer stabilized multiple Green Berets and Afghan Commandos who had suffered catastrophic trauma, including severed limbs, traumatic brain injuries, and paralysis, all while exposed on the sheer face of the mountain.

Facing imminent encirclement, Shurer rigged nylon tubular webbing around rocks and trees. Under direct enemy fire, he manually lowered four paralyzed and critically injured teammates down a 60-foot near-vertical cliff, using his own body as a physical shield to deflect incoming rounds and falling rock debris.

Shurer then helped carry the wounded across a freezing, raging river to the medevac landing zone, continuing to treat patients until every man was evacuated. Because of his actions, not a single American died on that mountain.

President Donald J. Trump presented Ronald J. Shurer II with the Medal of Honor on October 1, 2018.

After leaving the Army, Shurer continued his service to the nation as a Special Agent on the U.S. Secret Service Counter Assault Team (CAT). In May 2020, he tragically passed away from stage 4 lung cancer at the age of 41, leaving behind his wife Miranda and two young sons.

A true Green Beret. A warrior medic. An American hero.

The 23rd and 24th of June 2006 would be a crucible of leadership and heroism for an already battle-tested and decorated captain in the U.S. Army’s Special Forces. Captain Sheffield F. Ford III was in charge of some 16 Americans and 46 Afghan Army soldiers during "Operation Kaika" in the Panjawi District of Afghanistan’s Kandahar province.

In the bleak farmland, criss-crossed by ditches and barren expanses, Ford led his unit to "re-establish order" in the contested region, entering a Spartan Afghan village on the 23rd. The dilapidated buildings and mud huts were hiding a Taliban force of unknown strength with one thought on their minds: killing Americans and the Afghan soldiers working to take back their country. In their hastily prepared patrol base, Ford organized a perimeter as night enveloped the isolated Special Forces team and their Afghan allies.

As darkness fell, "all hell [broke] loose." From three directions, rifle, machine gun, and rocket-propelled grenade fire landed and exploded on their position. One of Ford’s squad mates later said they had "not seen this disciplined execution of infantry tactics" by the Taliban. Ford dug his men in to repel the assault.

Moving from position to position, he alternated between barking orders, firing at the enemy, and rallying the Afghan soldiers with him. As the night crept on, the remaining Taliban fighters withdrew and Ford took stock of the situation.

Early the next day, he ordered some of his Special Forces operators to lead a team of Afghans into the suspected Taliban hideout. As the unit engaged the hostiles, it was divided in two when some 200 Taliban fighters poured out, separating the American attackers and surrounding the make-shift patrol base.

Over the radio, Ford was connected with one of the translators who had been leading the mission on the Taliban position. The translator saw two Americans were fighting despite being severely wounded and feared capture at any minute. Knowing the ramifications of being taken alive by the Taliban, the translator told Ford he would, if ordered, end the suffering of the troops and his own life rather than be captured. Ford responded, "We’ve got people coming." Ford organized and launched an effective rescue to recover the translator and wounded troops, even if they were mortally wounded. He would not allow American or Afghan alike to be taken in any condition by the Taliban.

The adversaries fought so close to one another that the terrorists screamed to the Afghan soldiers that, "we can forgive you; just put your weapons down and walk away. We want the Americans alive." The months of training and the ties formed between the Americans and the Afghans were put to the test. Seeing the example of Ford running to each of the beleaguered fighters in the face of constant fire, and remembering all they had endured alongside their American trainers, the Afghan soldiers responded to the Taliban’s offer with well-aimed shots and an unbreakable defense.

Exemplifying the U.S. Special Forces motto, De Opresso Liber (to liberate the oppressed), Ford inspired his Afghan troops to stand up to the Taliban fighters and bring them down. He led an evacuation of all the men under his command, wounded included, out of the village under the cover of Apache attack choppers to ensure all would be safe, while sealing the fate of the insurgents. Ford successfully extricated his men, and the unit had more than 120 confirmed kills. Just as the Americans and Afghans had trained together, they sacrificed together; two American and three Afghan soldiers would not leave the battlefield alive. For his accomplishments in the face of such an overpowering force, Ford was awarded the Silver Star, the nation’s third highest military award.

SHOULD FIREARM SAFETY BE TAUGHT IN EVERY PUBLIC CLASSROOM? Tennessee has become the first state in the nation to mandate annual firearm safety classes for all public and charter school students from kindergarten through 12th grade. The landmark law aims to eliminate accidental childhood shootings by removing the dangerous curiosity around guns and teaching kids exactly what to do if they find an unsecured weapon.

“It will save kids, to be honest with you. It avoids some really bad situations. If we teach children from an early age never to touch a firearm and immediately alert an adult, we take away the curiosity that leads to tragedy.”

 Officer Chad Gann, Wildlife Officer & Firearm Instructor, Tennessee Department of Safety & Homeland Security

How the New Law Works
Statewide Annual Mandate: Under Tennessee Code Ann. § 49-6-1016, all public school districts and charter academies across Tennessee must deliver yearly age-appropriate firearm safety lessons developed in partnership with the Department of Education and the Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency (TWRA).

Elementary Curriculum (Grades K–5): Younger children focus strictly on accident avoidance and identifying real firearms versus toys. Lessons reinforce the foundational four-step rule: Stop, don't touch, leave the area, and immediately tell a trusted adult.

Middle & High School Curriculum (Grades 6–12): Older students study safe storage practices, the mechanical risks of handling firearms, hunter safety fundamentals, suicide prevention awareness, and the legal consequences of unlawful possession.

The state statute strictly prohibits live ammunition or working firearms during instruction. Certified School Resource Officers (SROs) and instructors use inert plastic training props, multimedia presentations, and classroom demonstrations.

Supporters emphasize that with over 400 million firearms in circulation across the United States, basic firearm safety is a vital life skill comparable to teaching kids how to swim, look both ways before crossing the street, or practice fire drills. Demystifying guns reduces accidental discharges caused by childish curiosity.

Critics and gun reform advocates contend that the burden of gun safety belongs exclusively on adult gun owners through strict safe-storage laws, arguing that mandatory school instruction risks normalizing weapons in learning environments.

The EFP had caused catastrophic damage to the vehicle in the rear of the column, which had the platoon medic and convoy commander in it. He directed his vehicle to be turned around to the disabled and burning Humvee. Ignoring the heavy volume of hostile fire, he leapt out to assist the trapped soldiers.
He bravely attempted to rescue the gunner of the Humvee, though temporarily overcome by smoke inhalation he recovered and joined another soldier in continuing the rescue. While doing so, he noticed the platoon's medic on the ground, badly wounded and Mora immediately began administering first aid. Once another soldier relieved him, Mora moved to the other side of the Humvee to cover his fellow soldiers.

It was then that he noticed that the gunner from the Humvee was finally free, but was bleeding heavily from his left leg. Mora swiftly applied a tourniquet to the leg to stop the bleeding. Realizing that they were in an exposed position, Mora and another sergeant took turns carrying the wounded gunner to safety, all while under fire from the insurgents. When reinforcements arrived, Mora helped to successfully evacuate the gunner to the Green Zone for medical care.

Because of his courageous actions and steadfast determination, Sergeant Ezequiel Mora helped save the lives of several of his fellow soldiers and as a result, was awarded the Bronze Star with Valor.

Luis Fonseca, from the 2nd Marine Expeditionary Brigade’s Task Force Tarawa, was awarded the Navy Cross for bravery during the battle of Al-Nasiriyah, Iraq, on March 23, 2003.
